passages.t: A gift of flour, oil and frankincense
passages.happening:
“When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, his offering must consist of fine flour. He is to pour olive oil on it, put frankincense on it, and bring it to Aaron’s sons the priests” (verses 1-2).

The priest takes a handful of the flour and oil, with all the frankincense, and burns it “as a memorial portion on the altar, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (verse 2).

“The remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The first offering in the book was an animal, burned whole. The second has no animal in it and no blood. It is bread, or the makings of bread: grain that someone grew, ground and mixed with oil. The text never says that it makes atonement. It is a gift.

The Hebrew word is minchah. In everyday speech it meant a present or tribute given to someone greater. Jacob's present to his brother Esau is called by this word. Here it is the gift a farmer brings to God from his own harvest.

It was not a cheap gift. Fine flour was the best part of the wheat, more costly than ordinary meal. Frankincense was a resin from trees that grow in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, carried in along long caravan routes.

Only a handful was burned. It is called the ‘memorial portion’, from the Hebrew verb ‘to remember’. The handful stood for the whole gift and brought the giver to God's remembrance.

The rest went to the priests as their food. Priests were given no farmland of their own, and the people's offerings were how they lived. It is called ‘most holy’, which meant it had to be eaten in the holy place (6:16).

The grain offering was often brought along with a burnt offering or a peace offering. Meat and bread together made up a whole meal in that world, and both were given to God. An evening grain offering was made at the temple each day. The Jewish afternoon prayer is still called Minchah after it.
passages.later:
The first offerings in the Bible are called by this word. Cain brought “some of the fruit of the soil as an offering to the LORD” (Genesis 4:3).

A psalm asks that prayer may rise as this offering did: “May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering” (Psalm 141:2).

In the book of Acts an angel tells a Roman officer named Cornelius, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God” (Acts 10:4). The word is the one the old Greek translation used for the memorial portion.

Paul points to the priests' share when he writes about supporting those who serve the church: “those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings” (1 Corinthians 9:13).
passages.asks: The grain offering gave back to God a part of what he had given through rain, soil and work. Ask whether you think of what you earn as yours alone, or as something received. And ask what it would look like to bring God the first and best of your work, and not what is left over.

passages.t: Baked, cooked on a griddle, or in a pan
passages.happening:
The offering may also be brought cooked. If it is “baked in an oven, it must consist of fine flour, either unleavened cakes mixed with oil or unleavened wafers coated with oil” (verse 4). If it is made on a griddle, it is unleavened bread mixed with oil, crumbled, with oil poured over it (verses 5-6). If it is cooked in a pan, it is fine flour with oil (verse 7).

Whichever way it is made, it is brought to the priest, who takes it to the altar (verse 8). He burns the memorial portion “as an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (verse 9). The rest belongs to Aaron and his sons (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
These three ways of cooking come straight from an ordinary kitchen. The oven was a clay cylinder heated from inside, with the dough pressed against its walls. Ovens of this kind are still used in villages across the Middle East. The griddle was a flat plate of clay or metal set over a fire. The pan was probably a deeper pot.

So a household could bring its own bread, made in its own way. Nothing here needs a herd or a flock. A family with a little flour and oil could bring a gift to God.

The passage speaks to the worshiper directly: ‘if you bring’. And after each kind it says the same simple thing: ‘it is a grain offering’. Baked, griddled or cooked in a pan, each is received in the same way. The pattern is the one chapter 1 used for the bull, the goat and the bird.

Verses 8 to 10 repeat the words of verses 2 and 3 almost exactly: the memorial portion, the pleasing aroma, and the rest for the priests. The ordinary work of a kitchen is taken up into worship.
passages.later:
Moses later gave Israel words to say when they brought the first of their harvest: “I have brought the firstfruits of the land that You, O LORD, have given me” (Deuteronomy 26:10).

The New Testament does not explain this chapter directly, but it uses the same kind of language for gifts with no blood in them. Paul calls a church's gift to him “a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). Hebrews says, “do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased” (Hebrews 13:16).
passages.asks: A family's own bread, made the way they always made it, could be brought to God. Ask what ordinary work of yours could be offered to him: a meal cooked, a job done well, a skill used for someone else. And ask whether you keep worship and daily work in separate rooms.

passages.t: No leaven or honey, always salt, and the first grain
passages.happening:
“No grain offering that you present to the LORD may be made with leaven, for you are not to burn any leaven or honey as an offering made by fire to the LORD” (verse 11). Leaven and honey may be brought as firstfruits, but they are not burned on the altar (verse 12).

“And you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt. You must not leave the salt of the covenant of your God out of your grain offering; you are to add salt to each of your offerings” (verse 13).

The first grain of the harvest is offered as crushed heads of new grain, roasted in the fire, with oil and frankincense. The priest burns the memorial portion (verses 14-16).
passages.hearers:
Three rules cover every grain offering.

No leaven and no honey in the altar fire. Leaven is what makes dough rise. Honey here probably means fruit syrup as well as bees' honey. The chapter gives no reason for keeping them from the fire. Perhaps it is because both ferment and so are linked with decay. They were not bad in themselves. They could be brought as firstfruits, and the loaves offered at the Feast of Weeks were baked with leaven (23:17).

Always salt. Salt keeps food from spoiling, and in the ancient Near East it was a sign of something that lasts. People who shared salt at a meal were bound to one another. So the chapter calls it ‘the salt of the covenant of your God’. Every time an Israelite salted an offering, it was a small reminder that he stood inside a relationship with God that was meant to endure.

And the first grain. When the new harvest began, the first heads were roasted, crushed and offered. Giving the first part said that the whole harvest came from God, and it trusted him for the rest.
passages.later:
The phrase comes back for promises that last. God's gift of the holy offerings to the priests is “a permanent covenant of salt before the LORD” (Numbers 18:19), and the kingship was given to David and his descendants ‘by a covenant of salt’ (2 Chronicles 13:5).

Because leaven spreads through a whole batch of dough, it later became a picture of something that spreads unseen. Jesus warned, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). Paul told the church at Corinth to keep the feast “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8).

Jesus used salt as a picture for his followers: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13).
passages.asks: Every offering carried the salt of the covenant, a sign of faithfulness that does not spoil. Ask what in your life with God has lasted through the years, and thank him for it. And ask what is working through your life unseen, like leaven through dough, for good or for harm.
